doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

title: Practice habits, endurance and long tones
summary: He admits practicing less than he should; would work on long tones and intonation.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Yeah — uh not as much as Sam Kininger should. He practices a lot on the gigs. Yeah, that’s something I should definitely do a little more of.

I would think that most of the stuff you do it’s just as importance that you just have your endurance, you know. Because I know that as I have become more of a piano player that my embouchure wears out in a hurry.

In jazz it still does too, yeah, it definitely happens, where like halfway through the gig, if I haven’t — even for like a week or something like that. You know I’ll put a new reed on, you know and then in the middle of the gig I’m taking shorter solos — “Why don’t you take this one?” You know? But you have to stay in better condition. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
What would you, if you went home this afternoon and did a practice session, what would you practice?

Long tones. Because intonation is huge. You know I would try and practice intonation, yeah. Because I have a problem with the upper register and I always have, being sharp. So that’s what I would do. I would just practice tone. I wouldn’t get all crazy with it I would just try and do slow tunes. Simple. [long tone] Just to make sure that it’s the tone that you want also too. And then the range of the horn, obviously you go from top to bottom.
